space noun

beyond the earth’s air

also outer space, in space, the void

classical

Cic. Fin. 1.17: in īnfīnītō inānī
Lucr. 1.426: locus ac spatium, quod ināne vocāmus
M-O s.v. space (space travel): ināne īnfīnītum, after Egger

ināne, inānis n.

noun, third declension

empty space, the void

The void of Democritus and Epicurus, in which the atoms move (Lucretius, Cicero). Egger calls outer space ināne īnfīnītum, and sends spacecraft in ināne īnfīnītum (Morgan–Owens s.v. launch).

Other words

  • spatium cosmicum — outer space

    also used · modern · M-O s.v. space (space travel), after Egger

    Egger also writes ināne spatium cosmicum and spatium īnfīnītum (Morgan–Owens).

Examples

  • in īnfīnītō inānī, in quō nihil nec summum nec īnfimum nec medium nec ultimum nec extrēmum sit

    in an infinite void, in which there is no top or bottom, no middle, no end and no edgeCic. Fin. 1.17

  • tum porrō locus ac spatium, quod ināne vocāmus, sī nūllum foret, haut usquam sita corpora possent esse

    then again, if there were no room and space, which we call the void, bodies could not be anywhere at allLucr. 1.426–428

See also sky, star, space.

SourcesLewis & Short: inanis · Lewis & Short: spatium · Lewis & Short: cosmicus

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. space; launch (a spacecraft).

Cicero’s De finibus and Lucretius checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).

Traupman has no word for outer space.
